Diegetic and nondiegetic music, score, source music, motif, and leitmotif

claims.claim: Music is one component of film sound design and can relate to image, narrative, dialogue, effects, ambience, and editing through timing and contrast.
Musical accompaniment was part of many silent-era theatrical film experiences before synchronized sound became standard.
Diegetic music belongs to the story world available to characters, while nondiegetic music is presented for viewers outside that world.
A score is music composed for a moving-image work, while pre-existing songs or source music can be selected and may function diegetically or nondiegetically depending on the scene.
A recurring musical idea can function as a motif; when associated with a particular character, place, or idea, it can be analyzed as a leitmotif.
Formal viewing and listening can attend to music alongside sound effects, silence, dialogue, narrative ordering, rhythm, and pacing.

A responsible interpretation describes when music enters, changes, returns, or contrasts with an image, then makes a qualified contextual claim rather than assigning a fixed meaning to a genre, instrument, or cue.
